passages.happening:
‘Wisdom has built her house; she has carved out her seven pillars’ (verse 1). ‘She has prepared her meat and mixed her wine; she has also set her table’ (verse 2). She sends out her servant girls and calls from the heights of the city.

“Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” (verse 4). To anyone who lacks sense she says, “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed. Leave your folly behind, and you will live; walk in the way of understanding” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
This chapter brings the book's opening section to its climax. Since chapter 1 the young reader has heard two sets of voices: the father and Wisdom on one side, the gang and the forbidden woman on the other. Now the choice is set out as two rival feasts in the same public place, offered to the same passers-by in almost the same words.

Meat was a luxury, eaten mostly at festivals and sacrifices, so slaughtering animals for a feast meant a generous host and a great occasion. Wine was often mixed with water or spices as part of preparing a proper meal. Sending servant girls to call guests from the high places of the town was how a wealthy host gave invitations. Wisdom's feast is lavish, and it is open to all.

The seven pillars have been read several ways: a large, well-built house, since ordinary houses had few pillars; seven as the number of completeness; the pillars of the world; or, in later allegory, the days of creation or other sevens. The text does not explain the number, and it is wise not to build much on it. Some scholars hear an echo of ancient stories in which a god celebrates a finished house or temple with a feast. Others read it simply as a noble lady hosting a banquet.
passages.later: Isaiah pictures the LORD's own feast: ‘On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples’ (Isaiah 25:6). And he gives the same invitation: “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters” (Isaiah 55:1).
passages.asks: Wisdom's invitation is to the simple, not to the clever. Ask whether you have thought you needed to be wise already before you could come. And ask what folly she is asking you to leave behind at her door.

passages.t: The mocker, the wise, and where wisdom begins
passages.happening:
Between the two feasts stand a few sayings. ‘He who corrects a mocker brings shame on himself’ (verse 7). ‘Do not rebuke a mocker, or he will hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you’ (verse 8). ‘Instruct a wise man, and he will be wiser still’ (verse 9).

At the center is the book's motto again: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding” (verse 10).

‘For through wisdom your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life’ (verse 11). ‘If you are wise, you are wise to your own advantage; but if you scoff, you alone will bear the consequences’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The mocker, from the word luts, is the person who sneers at correction. He is the hardest case in the book, because he will not be taught. The wise person is the opposite. Correct him and he grows. Being teachable is itself a mark of wisdom.

Verse 10 repeats the motto of 1:7 with a small change, so that the whole opening section begins and ends with the fear of the LORD. It adds a phrase: knowledge of the Holy One. Holy, qadosh, means set apart, utterly other. Wisdom begins not only with reverence but with knowing God himself.

Verse 12 is a sober reminder that each person carries his own choices. The wise man's wisdom is his own gain, and the scoffer bears his own scorn.
passages.later: The psalmist asks to be corrected: ‘Let the righteous man strike me; let his rebuke be an act of loving devotion’ (Psalm 141:5). And the motto stands in the psalms too: ‘The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom’ (Psalm 111:10).
passages.hard:
Does verse 11 promise a longer life to everyone who is wise?

Verse 11 says that through wisdom your days will be multiplied. Like the promises in chapters 3 and 4, this is a proverb that describes how life tends to go. It is not a guarantee for every person.

Wise living does tend to protect people from violence, recklessness, addiction and many dangers that shorten lives, and the book's opening chapters have shown folly leading to early death. But Scripture also records wise and righteous people who died young, and Ecclesiastes says plainly that one fate comes to the wise and the foolish alike (Ecclesiastes 2:14-16).

Read as a promise that the faithful never die early, the verse would be cruel to grieving families. Read as a proverb, it is a true picture of the direction wisdom takes a life. No one should tell a family that someone they loved died young for lack of wisdom.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The wise love the person who corrects them. Ask how you take a rebuke, and whether anyone feels free to correct you. And ask what it would mean to know the Holy One, not only to know about him.

passages.t: Folly's doorway and her stolen water
passages.happening:
‘The woman named Folly is loud; she is naive and knows nothing’ (verse 13). She sits at the door of her house, on a seat on the heights of the city, calling to people who are walking straight along their way (verses 14-15).

She uses Wisdom's very words: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” (verse 16). But her offer is different: “Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is tasty!” (verse 17).

‘But they do not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Folly's setup looks like Wisdom's, but it is cheaper and more hidden. She has no servants and no feast. She sits at her own door and calls out. And she offers stolen water and bread eaten in secret.

In a land where water was carefully owned and guarded (5:15-16), stolen water meant pleasure taken from what belongs to someone else, most likely another man's wife. The thrill of the forbidden is the whole of her offer.

The two invitations begin with the same words. The difference is in what follows. Wisdom offers bread, wine, life and understanding. Folly offers stolen pleasure, and her house is full of the dead, the rephaim, the shades of Sheol. Her guests do not know where they are sitting.

After this chapter the book turns to its collections of short sayings. Chapter 9 is the doorway. A reader has to accept Wisdom's invitation for the sayings that follow to do their work.
passages.later: Moses set the same choice before Israel: ‘I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life, so that you and your descendants may live’ (Deuteronomy 30:19).
passages.asks: Folly's offer is sweet because it is stolen. Ask whether there is some pleasure you want partly because it is forbidden. And ask which of the two doorways in this chapter you have been sitting near.
